theme: Coaching as the Core Manager Behavior
title: The Growth Record
titleHtml: Put your growth on the record.
tagline: Capturing your development goals and career-conversation notes in Oracle.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for all Vanderbilt staff: put your development goals into Oracle, keep useful notes from the career conversations you are part of, and make your growth visible enough for opportunity to find it.
heroLead: Goals set in good career conversations often stay unwritten. This session shows you how to put them in Oracle, where reviews and project staffing can actually find them.
objectives: Enter one real development goal in Oracle, written so a reader can act on it
Keep a short, useful note after any career conversation you are part of
Sort what belongs on your visible record, in private notes, or nowhere at all
missionTie: A university out to define the century can only see the ambitions its people write down, and every goal on the record strengthens Exceptional Core Operations from the inside.

agenda.d: Who actually reads your record, and what a written goal buys you.
Oracle, your own notes, or nowhere: the five-second sort.
One goal and one conversation note, written so they still work in six months.

manifesto: Write your development goal in Oracle: a direction plus a dated first step.

sections.headline: Write the goal where readers can find it.
sections.lead: When a stretch project or a Transfer Portal opening appears, someone looks at the record to see who is reaching for what, and a goal that lives in your head is invisible to that search. Writing it into Oracle is how you raise your hand in advance.

source.label: LinkedIn Workplace Learning Report: career goals and retention

sections.group: In pairs: name a goal you are carrying that exists nowhere in writing. What would change if the right person could see it?
sections.solo: Name a goal you are carrying that exists nowhere in writing. What would change if the right person could see it?

deeper.title: The readers you never meet
deeper.body: Your record has more readers than your manager: talent reviews, project leads staffing a stretch assignment, whoever hands out course seats. LinkedIn's Workplace Learning Report found that people who set career goals engage with learning about four times as much, and that development is now the first retention move organizations reach for. A written goal is what lets that machinery find you. Write for readers you have not met.
steps: Open your Oracle profile and read it as a stranger would. Note what a project lead could actually act on; it is usually less than you think.
Draft one goal for a reader you have never met: the direction you want, plus a first step with a date.

interaction.context: Take a quick chat poll before any teaching: how many of you carry a career goal that exists nowhere in writing? Every quiet hand is a goal no talent review or staffing search can find. The readers who decide those things can only see what is written down.
interaction.discuss: What has kept your goals unwritten so far? And who is one reader, named by role, you would actually want to find them?

card.text: Managers, mentors, and internal recruiters can only work with what they can see. A goal written in Oracle stays visible in the reviews and staffing decisions you are never in the room for; a goal in your head is invisible to all of them.

interaction.q: You want to move toward data work within two years. Where does that ambition do the most for you?

opts.t: In your head until a data role is actually posted
opts.why: By posting day the shortlist is often half-formed. The record works earliest, before the opening exists, when projects and course seats get handed out.

opts.t: Written as a development goal in Oracle
opts.why: Right. On the record it can surface in talent reviews, project staffing, and course nominations, whether or not you are in the room.

opts.t: Mentioned to your manager once at review time
opts.why: A good start with a short shelf life. Spoken goals fade with busy seasons and manager changes; written ones survive both.

sections.headline: Some notes belong in Oracle. Some never will.
sections.lead: You will sit in career conversations all year: 1:1s, mentoring chats, peer feedback. Some of what you hear belongs on your visible record, some in your private notes, and some should never be written anywhere. The sort takes five seconds once you know it.
sections.group: In pairs: one thing you would happily put on your visible record, and one thing you would keep in private notes. Compare sorts.
sections.solo: Write one thing you would put on your visible record and one thing you would keep in private notes.

deeper.title: The gray shelf
deeper.body: The three shelves get tested by gray cases. Feedback you received is yours and raw at once: hold it in private notes until you can write the pattern in your own words, then move the pattern to Oracle. Agreements that involve someone else: record your side and your commitments; theirs are theirs to write. For anything that still will not sort, one test settles it: would you be glad to have it read back to you in a year?
steps: Sort every takeaway from your last three career conversations onto a shelf: Oracle, private notes, or unwritten.
Take your grayest case and run the test: would you be glad to have it read back to you in a year?

interaction.intro: After each conversation, you decide where the takeaway lives. Read each one and sort it.
labels: Nowhere. Do not write it down
interaction.passMsg: You have the sort. Goals and agreed actions go visible; raw self-observations stay yours; other people's private business stays unwritten.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: your goals and agreed next steps go visible, your raw reflections stay private, and other people's disclosures are never yours to record.

items.q: You and your manager agree you will lead the spring onboarding revamp as a stretch toward project management.
items.why: An agreed development action is exactly what the record is for. Written in Oracle, it becomes evidence of growth when roles and projects open up.

items.q: After a tense meeting, you want to note that you went quiet when a senior director challenged your numbers.
items.why: Honest self-observation fuels growth and deserves privacy while it is raw. Keep it in your own notes; share the pattern later, in your own words, if you choose.

items.q: In a mentoring chat, a colleague mentions a health situation that is draining their energy this term.
items.why: Private information about another person is never yours to record, in any system, under any label. Hold it with care and write nothing.

sections.headline: Write it so a reader can act.
sections.lead: A growth record is only as useful as its writing. 'Improve communication' gives a reader nothing to act on. Donald Sull's goal research at MIT Sloan is the standard here: specific and visible beats vague. Write a direction, a dated step, the agreement.

source.label: With Goals, FAST Beats SMART, Donald Sull (MIT Sloan)

deeper.title: Keep the record alive
deeper.body: The first entry is the easy part; records die of staleness. A goal from two roles ago reads worse than no goal at all, because it tells a reader you stopped tending the page. So sweep quarterly: retire what no longer pulls you, sharpen dates that slipped, and add the agreement from your latest career conversation. Before any career conversation, open your last note first. The follow-up line is your agenda, already written.
steps: Put a recurring fifteen-minute hold on your calendar named 'record sweep' and run the first one this week.
Before your next 1:1, open your last conversation note and let its follow-up line set the first agenda item.

interaction.intro: You just had a good career conversation. Capture it in two fields: the goal and the note.

opts.coach: Too foggy to feed. No reader can hand this goal a project, a course, or an introduction; it will sit in Oracle politely doing nothing.

opts.t: Get better at presenting to leadership audiences.
opts.coach: A real direction now. Add the first step you are taking and it becomes something a manager or mentor can actually respond to.

opts.t: Present to a leadership audience twice this year; first rep at the May ops review.
opts.coach: Direction plus a dated first step. A reader knows exactly what you want and how to help; that is a goal that attracts opportunity.

opts.t: Great chat with my manager about my future.
opts.coach: Warm, and useless by Thursday. No date, no agreement, no next step; in six months this note is a pleasant mystery.

opts.t: Mar 1:1: we discussed my interest in project work.
opts.coach: Dated and topical, which future you will appreciate. It still lacks the agreement, which is the part everyone forgets first.

opts.t: Mar 1:1: agreed I shadow the onboarding project through April; revisit in May 1:1.
opts.coach: Date, agreement, follow-up. This note runs the next conversation for you and quietly holds everyone to what was said.

heads.strong: A record that works while you sleep. A clear goal, a dated agreement, and a follow-up already on the calendar.
heads.mid: A decent record with soft edges. The direction is there; the agreements will depend on everyone's memory.
heads.weak: Oracle has words in it. Six months from now they will tell you nothing and show a reader even less.

reactions.strong: In April, a project lead searching for presentation-hungry staff finds your goal and offers you the May ops review slot. The note means the shadow agreement holds without anyone being reminded.
reactions.mid: The May 1:1 opens with 'remind me what we said?' You rebuild half the agreement from memory, and the May rep quietly slips to fall.
reactions.weak: A talent review skims your profile and moves on; there was nothing to act on. The onboarding shadow never happens, and nobody notices it was ever discussed.

recap.q: Where does a development goal do the most for your career?
opts: In your head, ready when asked
recap.why: Visible goals surface in staffing, nominations, and reviews you are never in the room for. The other three wait to be asked.

recap.q: A colleague shares a private struggle in a mentoring chat. You should...
opts: Note it in Oracle for context
Add it to your private notes
Write nothing; hold it with care
Mention it to their manager quietly
recap.why: Other people's private information is never yours to record anywhere. Your record is for your own goals and agreements.

recap.q: What makes a conversation note useful in six months?
opts: Staying vague to keep options open
recap.why: Those three parts let the note run your next conversation and hold agreements without anyone leaning on memory.

recapMsgs.high: You have the sort and the writing. Now put the real entry in Oracle.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Revisit the section you missed, then draft your entry.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: One goal, on the record, this week.
capstone.lead: Draft the entry here, then put the real thing in Oracle before the week ends. Nothing you type on this screen is saved or sent; the Oracle entry is the one that counts.
capstone.whoLabel: Your goal, in one sentence a reader could act on.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. lead a cross-department project this year; first step booked by April

practices.name: The dev goal
practices.move: Enter one development goal in Oracle: a direction plus a dated first step.

practices.name: The conversation note
practices.move: After your next career conversation, write the date, the agreement, and the follow-up while it is fresh.

practices.name: The record sweep
practices.move: Open your Oracle profile, retire what is stale, and make sure what is there reads like you today.

whens.out: The entry goes into Oracle today, before the session's momentum fades.
The entry is in Oracle by Friday, with fifteen minutes blocked on the calendar to do it.
Your next 1:1 ends five minutes early so the goal and the note go straight into Oracle.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did writing it down make clearer about what you actually want?

closing.headline: Put the goal in Oracle this week.
closing.lead: Move the drafted goal from your card into Oracle this week. Thursday closes the week with the listening skill underneath every good career conversation.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextBody: Move your drafted goal from the card into Oracle exactly as built: a direction and a dated first step. Then note your next career conversation the same day it happens.
closing.brandline: Enter the goal in Oracle this week.

facilitator.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; no one is assumed to manage people. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; March is the Coaching as the Core Manager Behavior month, and this session gives every staff member the record side of it.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Is your development goal in Oracle? Did you note your last career conversation? What did writing it down make clearer?' Count of new Oracle goals is the month's adoption signal for the record.

s1.title: Why the record matters
s1.purpose: Establish visibility as the point: goals in Oracle keep working when you are out of the room.
s1.say: Quick show of hands in chat: how many of you have a career goal that exists nowhere in writing? That is normal, and it has a cost. When stretch projects and internal openings get decided, someone is looking at a record, and a goal that lives in your head is invisible to that search. LinkedIn's Workplace Learning Report backs the habit we build today: people who write their career goals down engage with their own development about four times as much. Writing it down is how you raise your hand in rooms you are not in.
facilitate: Run the chat show of hands first; the count of unwritten goals makes the visibility point concrete.
Read the visibility rule from the card, then share the In the room card and let the count sink in.
Run the discussion prompt, then the breakout on the goal that exists nowhere in writing.

ask.q: What has kept your goal out of Oracle so far?
expect: Never thought of Oracle as mine to use
It reads like HR paperwork, so it never felt urgent
ask.respond: All common. Today reframes the record as a tool you point at your own future, and the sort in the next section handles the exposure worry directly.

s1.debrief: Visible goals get fed; invisible ones wait, and nobody knows they are waiting.
s1.watchFor: Staff who assume this is a managers-only tool. Say it plainly: every field in this session is yours, whoever you report to.
s1.transition: So some things go on the record. The next skill is knowing what does.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; take the unwritten-goal count from chat and move.

s2.title: What goes where
s2.purpose: Install the three-shelf sort: visible record, private notes, or never written.
s2.say: You will be in career conversations all year, your own and other people's. The sort has three shelves. Goals and agreed actions go in Oracle, visible. Raw self-observations belong in your private notes, because honesty needs a little privacy while it is fresh. Other people's private business goes nowhere, ever. Five seconds of sorting protects you and everyone around you.
facilitate: Run System, notes, or nowhere? live; everyone sorts on their own screen.
Pause after round three; let the 'write nothing' answer breathe before you move.
Run the breakout: one thing for the visible record, one for private notes.

ask.q: Why does round three, the colleague's health situation, get 'write nothing' rather than private notes?
expect: It is theirs to tell, never mine to store
Notes get seen, forwarded, or found
Writing it down would change how I treat them
ask.respond: All of it. Your private notes are for your own growth. Other people's disclosures are held in trust, and trust does not have a text field.

s2.debrief: Yours and agreed goes visible; yours and raw stays private. Other people's private business is never yours to write.
s2.watchFor: The quiet worry that the visible record gets used against people. Name it: the record is for growth and mobility, and section three shows how to write entries you would be glad to have read.
s2.transition: You know what goes in. Now we make what goes in worth reading.
s2.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one sort question from chat.

s3.title: Write the entry
s3.purpose: Turn goals and notes into entries a future reader can act on: direction, date, agreement, follow-up.
s3.say: Oracle rewards a particular kind of writing, and it is teachable in one line: write so a reader can act. 'Improve communication' gives a reader nothing. 'Present to a leadership audience twice this year, first rep at the May ops review' gives them everything: what you want, when it starts, how to help. Donald Sull's research at MIT Sloan lands in the same place: specific goals beat 'do your best' by a wide margin, and goals work harder when other people can see them, which is the whole point of writing yours into Oracle. Same with notes. Date, agreement, follow-up, and the note runs your next conversation for you.
facilitate: Run Build your entry; two minutes for both fields, then save it.
Ask one volunteer to read their six-months-later outcome aloud.
Point at the pattern: direction plus dated step for goals; date plus agreement plus follow-up for notes.

ask.q: What makes 'improve my communication skills' so common and so useless?
expect: It is safe and cannot be wrong
It came off a review form, never from a real want
ask.respond: Safe is the problem: it is a goal nothing can respond to. Specific goals feel exposed for a week and get fed for a year.

s3.debrief: Write for the reader who wants to help you. A direction, a dated first step, and notes that hold the agreement.
s3.watchFor: Perfectionism stalling the entry. A rough goal in Oracle beats a polished one in your head, and it can be edited forever.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you draft the real entry.
s3.coreNote: Core: everyone builds solo; skip the read-aloud.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now draft the real thing. One development goal, written so a reader could act on it, and pick when it goes into Oracle. The card is your draft; the Oracle entry this week is the actual capstone. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: Your card is a draft; the entry in Oracle is the real finish line, so get it there this week. Thursday's Thrive Thursday closes the coaching week with the skill underneath every conversation you will ever capture: empathy, hearing what isn't said. And if you are working through this month's LinkedIn Learning pick, Sara Canaday's Coaching Skills for Leaders and Managers, the note habit you built today is exactly where the navigator-led GROW practicum conversations belong.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: Someone says their manager never looks at Oracle
contingencies.then: True sometimes, and the record still works: talent reviews, project staffing, and internal recruiters search it whether or not one manager does. Write for the readers you cannot see.

contingencies.if: Someone starts typing a real colleague's private situation into chat as an example
contingencies.then: Redirect immediately and warmly: 'Roles, never names, and other people's private business stays unwritten, here included.' Then restate the three-shelf sort.

toughQuestions.q: Who can actually see what I enter in Oracle?
toughQuestions.a: Your manager and the talent teams who run reviews and staffing; each field shows its visibility if you are unsure. The working rule keeps you safe either way: write every visible entry as if a future hiring manager will read it, because the useful ones will.

toughQuestions.q: What if my goal is to move away from my current team?
toughQuestions.a: Mobility goals are legitimate; internal movement is exactly what the record and the Transfer Portal support. Frame the direction rather than the departure: 'grow toward project leadership' works on the record, and the specifics stay in conversations you choose to have.

toughQuestions.q: I'm not a manager, so is the coaching month really for me?
toughQuestions.a: Yes. Coaching is two-sided: managers are learning to ask this month, and a visible record gives them something real to ask about. Written goals make you easy to coach and easy to advocate for, whoever you report to.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Tuesday, 45 minutes to put your growth on the record. Bring one career goal you have never written down, and your Oracle login if you have it handy. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Is it in Oracle? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Is your development goal in Oracle? 2) Did you note your last career conversation? 3) What did writing it down make clearer?
